comments.author: @coachgomes
comments.text: The Island of Corvo may have more cows, and sheep than humans. The video mentions many times that there are only about 400 people who live there. I'm positive there are more herbivores on Corvo Island than people. I was born on Flores island in 1964, and my first language was European Portugueses. Each of the 9 islands have their own accent when speaking Portuguese. When meeting someone new, my father could tell which Island they were from based on their accent as they spoke Português. We immigrated to central California in April of 1966 when I was only 1.5 years old. We have immigration papers from the 1890's that my father's grandfather had kept throughout the years. He, and his 6 or 7 bothers immigrated and came on a ship to the San Francisco Harbor that sailed around Cape Horn at the tip of Souther America in the 1890's. The way of life on Corvo, Flores, and most all of the Azores is always all about cows, milk and meat. There were very few jobs on those islands where you made money to buy things or food. The way of life in the history of the world was to raise live stock. Cows, pigs, sheep, chickens, goats, and the fish in the sea was the job at hand. And you had a mom and a grandmother that baked bread almost everyday. You were born into a family that has been there for hundreds of years before you were born. And caring for the animals was what sustains your life. You need to eat: milk, cheese, meat, eggs, bread, drink water, coffee, wine, vegetables, soups, stews, and fruits. The seafood is abundant and free in the Atlantic Ocean that surrounds those islands. We took a small shuttle boat from Flores, to Fial, to Terceira Island in March of 1966. We flew over in a jet plane from Terceira Island to New York's Elise Island for immigration reasons in April of 1966. How the money was raised is by the cows that were auctioned off to the main land of Portugal. The main land of Portugal is very dry and thirsty for water, meat, and milk. The further west those islands are, the more rain, fog and bad weather happens on all those islands. It rains over 80inches of rain on Corvo and Flores. The further east the islands are, then the less rain they get. The most eastern Island is São Miguel, and it gets the least amount of rainfall of all the 9 islands. On São Miguel, it's warmer and dryer throughout the year. They grow pineapples and Jalapeños on São Miguel in a green house that keeps those plants nice and hot for them to grow in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. My grandfather on my mother's side, would eat raw Jalapeños picked off the plants. And he had a very different accent from the island of São Miguel. I have story and after story of life on those islands.

comments.text: 1 - I sincerely hope someone soon will bother to make you aware of the difference between a state, a continent and a tectonic plate. No matter how convincingly you try to intone it, a continent is not a state from which you can have a passport (as suggested) and a tectonic plate is not a continent even if christened after a continent that sits on it (North America and the North American Plate are different things). For information, the exact same geological processes are at the origin of the archipelago’s nine islands, and the picture is a bit more complex than you’ve portrayed it. 2 -  The Azores Triple Junction (ATJ) is a geologic triple junction where the boundaries of three tectonic plates intersect: the North American Plate, the Eurasian Plate and the African Plate. However, geologists explain the ATJ doesn’t mean the three plates meet at a point. There is enough proof to admit the existence of a microplate, commonly referred to as the Azores Microplate. In other words, the islands don’t sit on any of the three major plates. They sit on a microplate of their own. Even at a deep geological level, they are isolated alright.
